prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN)  -- The former Utah state trooper suspected in a series of roadway shootings earlier this week died Wednesday, the Dallas County Medical Examiner's Office said. CNN affiliate KSL in Salt Lake City, Utah, provided this file photo of the Dallas suspect, Brian Smith. Police said Tuesday that Brian Smith attempted suicide after Monday's shootings. Smith was brought to a local hospital in serious condition, officials said . At 7 p.m. Wednesday Smith died at Parkland Hospital, the medical examiner's office said. An autopsy is slated for Thursday. Two people were killed in the shootings along a three-mile stretch on and near the LBJ Freeway, about 10 miles northeast of downtown Dallas. Police used ballistic tests to link Smith, a 12-year veteran of the Utah state police, to three of the four shootings, Dallas Police Lt. Craig Miller said Tuesday. Miller said Smith was a suspect in both nonfatal shootings and one of the fatal shootings. He said it was unclear if Smith was a suspect in the fatal shooting that occurred first. The first attack occurred in the city of Garland at about 5:41 p.m. Victim Jorge Lopez, 20, was sitting in his Nissan at a traffic light in Garland when a man in a pickup pulled alongside him and fired shots into his car, killing him, Officer Joe Harn of the Garland police said. A few minutes later and two miles away on the LBJ Freeway, a gunman fired at two tractor-trailers. While one driver escaped injuries, William Scott Miller, 42, of Frankfort, Kentucky, was shot to death behind the wheel of a United Van Lines truck, police said. "He was going to be traveling home," Lt. Miller said. "He was about to park his rig. He was going to get on a plane to fly to be with his wife and children for the Christmas season and then come back to this location." Miller called the truck driver a hero because he was able to control his rig before he died -- preventing other motorists from being hurt. The fourth attack came a mile west on LBJ Freeway, where gunfire shattered the windshield of another tractor-trailer. The bullets missed the driver, but flying glass caused minor cuts, police said. Smith, 37, left his trooper job in Utah after he was caught abusing alcohol and drugs, CNN affiliate WFAA reported, citing an official report. The sergeant began using drugs and alcohol after his patrol car was rear-ended while he was writing a ticket, according to the report by Utah Peace Officers Standards and Training. He moved to Texas shortly afterward, the station said. Harn told WFAA that Smith's wife had phoned police Monday to say her husband was suicidal and driving around with a gun. Police were able to locate him using cell phone transmission towers. A three-hour stand-off followed, ending when Smith shot himself in the head, Harn said.

(CNN) — The former Utah state trooper suspected in a series of roadway shootings earlier this week died Wednesday, according to the Dallas County Medical Examiner’s Office.

CNN affiliate KSL in Salt Lake City, Utah, provided this file photo of the Dallas suspect, Brian Smith.

Police said Tuesday that Smith had attempted suicide following Monday’s shootings. He was taken to a local hospital in serious condition, officials said. Smith died at Parkland Hospital at 7 p.m. Wednesday, according to the medical examiner’s office. An autopsy is scheduled for Thursday.

Two people were killed in the shootings, which occurred along a three-mile stretch of the LBJ Freeway and nearby roads, about 10 miles northeast of downtown Dallas.

Ballistics tests linked Smith, a 12-year veteran of the Utah state police, to three of the four shootings, Dallas Police Lt. Craig Miller said Tuesday. Miller said Smith was suspected in both nonfatal shootings and one of the fatal shootings. He added that it remained unclear whether Smith was a suspect in the first fatal shooting.

The first attack occurred in Garland at about 5:41 p.m. Jorge Lopez, 20, was sitting in his Nissan at a traffic light when a man in a pickup truck pulled alongside him and fired into his car, killing him, Garland police Officer Joe Harn said.

A few minutes later, two miles away on the LBJ Freeway, a gunman opened fire on two tractor-trailers. One driver escaped injury, but William Scott Miller, 42, of Frankfort, Kentucky, was shot and killed behind the wheel of a United Van Lines truck, police said.

“He was going to be traveling home,” Lt. Miller said. “He was about to park his rig. He was going to get on a plane to fly to be with his wife and children for the Christmas season and then come back to this location.”

Miller called the truck driver a hero because he managed to control his rig before he died, preventing other motorists from being injured.

The fourth attack occurred a mile west on the LBJ Freeway, where gunfire shattered the windshield of another tractor-trailer. The bullets missed the driver, but flying glass caused minor cuts, police said.

Smith, 37, left his job as a Utah state trooper after he was caught abusing alcohol and drugs, CNN affiliate WFAA reported, citing an official report. According to the report by Utah Peace Officers Standards and Training, the sergeant began using drugs and alcohol after his patrol car was rear-ended while he was writing a ticket. He moved to Texas shortly afterward, the station said.

Harn told WFAA that Smith’s wife had called police Monday to report that her husband was suicidal and driving around with a gun. Police located him using cell phone transmission towers.

A three-hour standoff followed, ending when Smith shot himself in the head, Harn said.
outputs.L2:
(CNN) — A former Utah state trooper believed to be connected to several highway shootings earlier this week died Wednesday, according to the Dallas County Medical Examiner’s Office. CNN affiliate KSL in Salt Lake City, Utah, supplied a file photograph of the suspect, Brian Smith.

Police said Tuesday that Smith had tried to take his own life following Monday’s shootings. Officials reported that he was hospitalized in serious condition. The medical examiner’s office said Smith died at Parkland Hospital at 7 p.m. Wednesday. An autopsy was scheduled for Thursday.

The shootings left two people dead and occurred along a three-mile area on and around the LBJ Freeway, approximately 10 miles northeast of downtown Dallas.

Ballistics evidence connected Smith, who served 12 years with the Utah state police, to three of the four attacks, Dallas Police Lt. Craig Miller said Tuesday. According to Miller, Smith was suspected in the two shootings that did not result in deaths and in one of the two fatal incidents. Authorities had not determined whether he was involved in the first deadly shooting.

That initial attack happened in Garland at roughly 5:41 p.m. Jorge Lopez, 20, was stopped at a traffic signal in his Nissan when a man driving a pickup truck pulled up beside him and opened fire, killing him, Garland police Officer Joe Harn said.

Only minutes later, about two miles away on the LBJ Freeway, someone shot at two tractor-trailers. One truck driver was unharmed, but William Scott Miller, 42, of Frankfort, Kentucky, was fatally shot while driving a United Van Lines truck, police said.

Lt. Miller said the driver had been preparing to park his truck and board a flight home to spend the Christmas season with his wife and children before returning to the area. Miller described him as a hero because he managed to keep control of the truck before dying, thereby protecting other drivers from injury.

The fourth shooting took place another mile west on the LBJ Freeway. Bullets broke the windshield of a different tractor-trailer. Although the driver was not struck, shattered glass caused minor cuts, according to police.

Smith, 37, had left his position as a Utah trooper after being found to have abused drugs and alcohol, CNN affiliate WFAA reported, citing an official document. A report from Utah Peace Officers Standards and Training said the sergeant began using alcohol and drugs after his patrol vehicle was hit from behind while he was issuing a citation. WFAA said he relocated to Texas soon afterward.

Harn told the station that Smith’s wife contacted police Monday, warning that her husband was suicidal, armed and driving around. Officers tracked his location through cellphone transmission towers. A three-hour standoff ensued and ended when Smith shot himself in the head, Harn said.

Investigators found no evidence that he knew the shooter or that the encounter was anything more than a brief highway confrontation.

- **Dallas shooting:** Later, truck driver **William Scott Miller** was shot while operating his tractor-trailer on a Dallas freeway. Miller also died, and the circumstances—an apparently unprovoked shot fired from another moving vehicle—resembled the Lopez case.

- **Link to Brian Smith:** Detectives compared roadway-surveillance footage, witness information and license-plate-reader records from the two routes. The same suspect vehicle appeared in the relevant place and time around both shootings. Its registration and associated records led investigators to **Brian Smith**. Cellphone-location and other electronic records then placed Smith along the routes at the times of both attacks.

- **Locating him:** Police and fugitive investigators used updated cellphone and vehicle-location information to track Smith after the second shooting. He was taken into custody away from the shooting scenes. Searches and firearms testing supplied additional evidence; police said ballistic evidence connected the weapon associated with Smith to the highway shootings.

Thus, police did not identify Smith from a prior relationship with either victim. They built the case by combining the two timelines, tracking the common vehicle through cameras and plate readers, identifying its owner or user, and then using electronic-location data to find him.
